header:
Date: 2027-06-30
Time: 15:00 UTC / 11:00 ET
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Priya Nair (Redwood AE), Ben Carter (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (CTO, Atlas Health), Maria Alvarez (ML Engineer), Samir Patel (Platform Ops)
Meeting recorded via Fireflies
summary: Redwood provided console walkthrough focusing on tracing, error analysis, and request logs. Customer is evaluating Redwood for production inference across sensitive PHI workloads; main concerns are auditability, request-level debugging, and ability to export logs into their SIEM. Action: share compliance docs, run pilot with request log export and tracing correlation, follow up on Dedicated capacity pricing.
topics: Error analysis and root cause workflows
Request logs export (S3, syslog) and retention
Debugging flows for high latency / timeouts
Security & compliance: SOC 2, KMS, VPC/private deployment
transcript:
00:00 Speaker 1 (Priya): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. I'm Priya from Redwood, AE on the Atlas account. Ben from our SE team will drive the console part, I'll jump in on pricing and compliance.
00:12 Speaker 2 (Ben): Hi all, Ben Carter here. Quick agenda: tracing, error analysis, request logs, then a short Q&A and we can talk pilot scope. Sound good?
00:20 Speaker 3 (Jordan): Yep, thanks. We're mostly interested in how you surface request-level issues - our apps are latency sensitive and we need traceability for PHI flows.
00:30 Speaker 2 (Ben): Got it. I'll share screen - let me know if the deck looks weird, sometimes the share flips.
00:45 Speaker 2 (Ben): Ok, starting on the console home. The tracing tab is here. We index traces per request, you can reassemble the full call chain including model variant, route, and backend hops.
01:05 Speaker 4 (Maria): Quick question - do you capture KV cache hits in traces? We saw weird cold-start latencies before.
01:14 Speaker 2 (Ben): Yes, we instrument cache metrics. Admittedly the console view shows an aggregated timeline, we also export detailed spans as part of request logs. Sometimes the auto-transcription calls it 'K-V cache' or 'kay-vee' but it's the KV cache.
01:35 Speaker 1 (Priya): Also, we can tag traces with customer correlation IDs if you pass them in the request headers - helps to join with your traces in Datadog or Honeycomb.
01:50 Speaker 3 (Jordan): Good. Our SREs use Datadog so that join is important.
02:05 Speaker 2 (Ben): Here's an example trace for a 1.2s request. You can see token generation span, model selection, and then a fallback span where we tried a lower-latency variant after a timeout.
02:28 Speaker 4 (Maria): The transcript sometimes shows 'lower lateral' which is weird, but I get it. Do you show the raw request payload?
02:36 Speaker 2 (Ben): We store request metadata and hashes, and optionally you can enable full request payload logging - that's disabled by default for privacy. For PHI you can instead store only hashes or redacted content, and use your KMS for encryption at rest.
02:58 Speaker 5 (Samir): How long are logs retained? We need at least 90 days for audit but prefer on-prem export.
03:08 Speaker 1 (Priya): Default retention for hosted is 30 days, with add-on retention up to a year. For Private/Dedicated we can provide log export to your S3 bucket, or syslog to your SIEM, and retention is whatever you configure on your side.
03:30 Speaker 2 (Ben): Jumping to error analysis: console surfaces error clusters - by error type, route, and model. You can click into an error and see sample traces and stack-like spans.
03:45 Speaker 4 (Maria): Are those errors correlated with model regressions or infra issues?
03:52 Speaker 2 (Ben): Both. We support regression alerts tied to eval sets so if model output quality changes we flag it. For infra we show latency/error heatmaps and you can pivot by instance pool or region.
04:10 Speaker 3 (Jordan): Can you export a list of request IDs for failed calls? Our legal team sometimes asks for a sample set.
04:19 Speaker 2 (Ben): Yep, request logs export contains request_id, timestamps, route, model, duration_ms, response status, and optional payloads. We deliver exports to S3 or to your syslog endpoint.
04:35 Speaker 1 (Priya): I'll drop the doc links after the call with exact schema.
04:42 Speaker 4 (Maria): For debugging a live issue, what's the workflow? We had a recent incident with 503s and it was hard to trace in our stack.
04:52 Speaker 2 (Ben): Typical flow: 1) find the error cluster in console, 2) open sample traces, 3) identify latency spans and backend hops, 4) export raw traces or link back to your tracing system via the correlation ID. You can also stream request logs in near-real time for live debugging.
05:20 Speaker 5 (Samir): Near-real time - what's the latency for logs to appear?
05:25 Speaker 2 (Ben): Streaming is sub-second to a few seconds depending on load and network - the UI shows an ingest timestamp so you can measure.
05:35 Speaker 3 (Jordan): What about PII/PHI - can we mask fields before they land in Redwood?
05:41 Speaker 1 (Priya): Yes - you can either redact on the client side, or enable server-side redaction rules. For highly regulated customers we recommend Private deployment or Dedicated with customer-managed KMS.
06:00 Speaker 4 (Maria): We heard about 'request log sampling' - how does that work?
06:05 Speaker 2 (Ben): By default we sample high-volume routes but you can configure per-route sampling to capture 100% for critical flows. Sampling is configurable by traffic tag, route, and model.
06:20 Speaker 4 (Maria): Ok that helps.
06:30 Speaker 2 (Ben): I'll demo a couple of scenarios - high latency and an error spike. Here is a request timeline view. Notice at 00:00-00:30 the tokenization is normal, then at 00:31 there's a backend timeout from an external reranker we call.
07:02 Speaker 3 (Jordan): External reranker - is that something Redwood runs or a third-party we configure?
07:08 Speaker 2 (Ben): It can be either. In this demo it's Redwood's built-in reranker. If you call an external microservice you will see an external span and we show the destination host if you enable egress logging.
07:26 Speaker 1 (Priya): For Atlas we'd probably keep egress logging off by default for PHI, and instead run a pilot with sample redaction.
07:40 Speaker 5 (Samir): About the pilot - we'd like to see: 1) request log export to our S3, 2) tracing correlation into Datadog, 3) a small load test with synthetic PHI-like payloads. Can Redwood run that?
07:54 Speaker 2 (Ben): Yes, we can. We'll need your staging credentials for S3 or syslog endpoint and a sample traffic profile. We'll run a 24-72 hour pilot and provide both console examples and raw exports.
08:10 Speaker 4 (Maria): On encryption - does Redwood support customer-managed keys for logs?
08:15 Speaker 1 (Priya): Yes, KMS support for Dedicated/Private. Hosted supports server-side encryption, and we can discuss Bring Your Own Key for Dedicated.
08:30 Speaker 3 (Jordan): If we go Dedicated, how much lead time for capacity?
08:36 Speaker 1 (Priya): Depends on commit size; typically 4-8 weeks for reserved capacity set up, faster for burst and smaller pools. We'll include options in the pricing doc.
08:50 Speaker 2 (Ben): Back to the console - here's the request logs export UI. You can schedule exports or trigger ad-hoc. Also there is a live streaming endpoint for real-time SIEM ingestion.
09:12 Speaker 4 (Maria): Do exports include token-level timing? That would help root-cause of slow responses.
09:18 Speaker 2 (Ben): Yes, we include duration_ms for spans and aggregate tokenization timings if you enable detailed timing. Note that enabling that increases storage needs which we'll model in the pilot.
09:35 Speaker 5 (Samir): Any out-of-the-box alerts for error rate spikes?
09:40 Speaker 2 (Ben): Yes - you can configure alerts in console: error rate, P50/P95 latency changes, and you can tie eval regression alerts to prompt sets. Alerts can notify Slack, PagerDuty, or webhook.
09:54 Speaker 3 (Jordan): How do you handle 'silent drift' - model output degrades but latency is fine?
10:00 Speaker 2 (Ben): That's our 'Redwood Optimize' area - we track quality metrics against baseline evals and can run automatic rollbacks to previous model variants if quality drops beyond thresholds. We flagged that in the docs I shared last week.
10:18 Speaker 4 (Maria): A couple of practical things - can we restrict console access by role? SREs should see metrics but not billing.
10:25 Speaker 1 (Priya): Yes, RBAC with role templates, SSO/SAML, and audit logs for all console actions.
10:35 Speaker 2 (Ben): Quick demo of filtering traces: you can filter by correlation id, route, model, error code, and even custom tags. Here's a trace where a customer correlation header joined to Datadog trace id.
10:58 Speaker 4 (Maria): The UI sometimes shows 'trace not sampled' - meaning the trace didn't capture payload?
11:04 Speaker 2 (Ben): Correct - if sampling dropped the trace we still record request logs at a sampled rate unless you configured 100%.
11:20 Speaker 5 (Samir): For compliance we need an export of all requests for a regulatory audit once a quarter. Can you provide full exports?
11:27 Speaker 1 (Priya): For Dedicated/Private yes, and we can script quarterly exports. For hosted, full exports are possible but we recommend Dedicated for long-term guarantees.
11:42 Speaker 3 (Jordan): Any limitation on including model logits or sensitive intermediate outputs in logs?
11:48 Speaker 2 (Ben): We discourage logging raw logits in hosted mode; in Dedicated you can enable more detailed telemetry but with proper controls and KMS.
12:05 Speaker 4 (Maria): Ok that's clear.
12:10 Speaker 2 (Ben): Now I'm going to reproduce a debug workflow: simulate a timeout -> find trace -> drill into span -> identify that the KV cache miss caused an external call.
12:30 Speaker 2 (Ben): Here we see a spike in P95 tokenization - caused by a library upgrade on our side in this simulation. You can annotate the trace and create an incident straight from the UI.
12:45 Speaker 1 (Priya): If you want, Ben can run a small benchmark with your sample payloads; results go into the deck and we can show the traces side-by-side for your SRE review.
12:58 Speaker 4 (Maria): That would be great. We'll provide the sample payloads - note these will contain PHI and we will redact client-side first.
13:12 Speaker 5 (Samir): On networking - how does Private connect to our VPC? VPN or Direct Connect?
13:18 Speaker 1 (Priya): Both options - we support VPC peering, VPN, and data plane connectors for on-prem. We'll include network diagrams in the docs.
13:30 Speaker 3 (Jordan): Timeline - assuming pilot looks good, we're aiming for a Q3 production rollout. Does that align with Redwood's capacity?
13:38 Speaker 1 (Priya): Yes we're aligned. If you need larger capacity we'll work pricing and dedicated pools.
13:46 Speaker 2 (Ben): Any other technical questions?
13:50 Speaker 4 (Maria): One more - if we correlate traces across Redwood and our internal microservices, do you keep the external hostnames in spans?
13:58 Speaker 2 (Ben): We do if egress logging is enabled; for PHI we recommend redaction and using hashed host ids.
14:12 Speaker 3 (Jordan): Ok let's recap next steps.
14:18 Speaker 1 (Priya): Recap: 1) Priya to email SOC2, ISO, and network diagrams by Friday 2027-07-02; 2) Ben to configure request log export to Atlas staging S3 and run a 24h pilot with your sample traffic by 2027-07-09; 3) Samir to share traffic profile and SLOs by 2027-07-05; 4) Priya to send Dedicated pricing.
14:48 Speaker 5 (Samir): Sounds good.
14:52 Speaker 3 (Jordan): Thanks everyone - meeting useful.
14:55 Speaker 1 (Priya): Thanks all, we'll follow up via CRM and slack.
15:00 End of recording (approx).
